<reason>Both sides built plausible, well-grounded cases without resorting to fake citations. A's opening was strong on lock-in economics, continuity-of-care mechanics, and the counterintuitive point that weak buyers (rural districts, small hospitals) are most harmed by captivity, not helped by "turnkey" simplicity. But once A proposed its actual policy — a single-vendor turnkey delivery scored for open-interface compliance — B seized on this and relentlessly pressed the same structural critique across every round (B1.7 → B2.1 → B3.1 → B4.3 → B5.1): that this is functionally identical to B's own model of integration-plus-contract-discipline, meaning A never defended the resolution's actual "favor portability *over* integration" structure. A had a real answer available (a scored, cooperative-level certification regime is a structural market-wide default, not case-by-case haggling, and it specifically protects the one-IT-staffer district that cannot negotiate escrow clauses alone), and gestured at it in A2.4 and A5.4, but never drove the distinction home as sharply or as early as B's repeated pressure demanded. B's rebuttals were tighter, more consistently targeted at the resolution's wording, and better escalated round to round, giving the debate a cleaner throughline and making it easier to decide in B's favor, even though A's underlying substantive claims about lock-in risk were never fully neutralized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's recurring "you've conceded my case" critique (B2.1, sharpened in B3.1/B4.3, capstoned in B5.1) was the most decisive exchange: it forced A to spend its final speeches defending why a "turnkey system built on open locks" differs from B's own integration-plus-contract-terms model, a distinction A asserted but never fully proved.</best_rebuttal>
